science.qualification: Photosphere color from the star's Gaia DR3 BP/RP spectrum, dimmed toward the limb by the quadratic law Claret & Bloemen (2011), A&A 529, A75 compute from ATLAS model atmospheres for the Johnson V band at 4,781 K and log g 4.58 (u1 0.718, u2 0.069): a model, because no fit of this star's limb is used. The disc is unresolved: no map or absolute brightness is implied. Self-luminous, so no lighting.

science.label: Quarter 2
science.description: Brightness of the star's surface that reproduces its light as it turns once in 50.1 days, fitted with starry to the measured points of quarter 2 of the star's KEPSEISMIC light curve, which its authors make from the Kepler mission's pixels (the light varies by 0.25%; the map's curve leaves a scatter of 0.03%, the light's own noise being 0.01%). A light curve fixes how bright each longitude is, not the latitude of what darkens it. Santos et al. (2019, ApJS 244, 21) list the star as a rotator in their table (VizieR J/ApJS/244/21, table 3): a rotation period of 50.11 ± 6.67 d and a photometric activity (S_ph, the scatter of the light over five rotations) of 746 parts per million. The rotation and its period are theirs, taken as published; no criteria were applied to them here. The map is made at a tilt of 35°, worked out from the star's rotation speed, period and radius. Gaia DR3 lists 2 other stars within 16 arcseconds, with 1.5% of their light and the star's together. A reduction made in this project, not a published map.
science.title: Kepler · brightness map made here · Quarter 2

science.label: Color + brightness
science.description: The star's color (#ffcfad, its Color dataset) over the brightness map this project made from the star's light in Kepler quarter 16 (January to April 2013): the map's scale, 96% to 104% of the mean surface, runs from a darker, richer tone of the same hue to the color itself. The contrast is drawn far stronger than it is, so the parts can be told apart: the darkest part gives 6.1% less light than the brightest. Longitudes are fixed by the light curve; latitudes and shapes are not. No color change of the spots is drawn: none is measured. A reduction made in this project, not a published map.
science.title: Kepler · the star in its color over its brightness map · January to April 2013
